# SQLStructEval: Structural Evaluation of LLM Text-to-SQL Generation

[All reading notes](../reading-notes.md) · [Catalog entry](../README.md#sqlstructeval)

**Full paper read · 2026-11-09**

[Original source](https://aclanthology.org/2026.findings-aacl.122.pdf) · Findings of IJCNLP-AACL 2026 proceedings, pages 2404-2422

**Reading coverage:** All 19 PDF pages: Sections 1-6, limitations, Appendices A-G, Tables 1-8, Figures 1-4/captions, prompts, JSON/SQL examples and metric definitions. Figure 2 visually inspected.

## Research question

Explain differences in SQL structure among repeated outputs that can agree with a reference execution result.

## Method

Canonicalizes sqlglot-parsed queries and measures concentration, entropy, reference alignment and perturbation sensitivity. A JSON-to-SQL pipeline is compared with direct generation.

## Evaluation

Ten generations per question on Spider, three 100-question robustness subsets and 200 paraphrase/schema-order cases. Empty parsed/correct subsets contribute zero; reported averages therefore combine coverage with agreement.

## What the results support

The compile-style pipeline reports higher execution accuracy and correct-output concentration, while overall structural diversity increases. The result supports a diagnostic perspective, not a general preference for one canonical query.

## Limits and qualifications

Case-folding and limited alias handling are not semantic normalization. The pipeline comparison does not isolate compilation, and selected error-category samples do not estimate population error prevalence. Figure 2 labels a COUNT(1) grouping query incorrect despite its equivalence to the displayed COUNT(*) query.

## Relevance to reliable Text-to-SQL

Useful for inspecting alternative constructions; structural disagreement and single-database agreement do not establish semantic error or equivalence.
